# Innovations in Dockside Scheduling

Jessamy Dunkham: Welcome back to The Embix Review, where we explore cutting-edge tech reshaping industries. I’m Jessamy Dunkham, and today’s episode is all about innovations in dockside scheduling—specifically the new algorithms that are shaking up how ports manage their berths. Joining me is Xanthe Peltham, lead systems architect at Navisync, a firm pioneering AI-driven berth management solutions. Xanthe, great to have you here.

Xanthe Peltham: Thanks, Jessamy. Excited to dive into this—it’s a fascinating space right now.

Jessamy Dunkham: To start, could you lay out the core challenges ports face today with berth scheduling? What makes this problem so complex?

Xanthe Peltham: Absolutely. At a glance, it’s about allocating limited dock space to vessels that vary wildly in size, cargo type, and arrival time. But beneath that are layers of unpredictability—weather delays, customs clearance holdups, even crane breakdowns. For example, at Port Everbay, they had a week last July where a single crane failure cascaded, delaying over 20 container ships and causing berth conflicts three times over. Traditional scheduling relied heavily on static timetables and manual adjustments, which just can’t keep pace with real-time disruptions.

Jessamy Dunkham: So that’s where these new algorithms come in?

Xanthe Peltham: Exactly. We’re talking about adaptive systems that incorporate telemetry data from cranes, sensor inputs on container movement, and live customs clearance updates. Navisync’s latest algorithm, HarborFlow, uses a reinforcement learning model to anticipate delays and dynamically reshuffle berth assignments in real time.

Jessamy Dunkham: Can you give us an example of HarborFlow in action?

Xanthe Peltham: Sure! At the Port of Westmoor last December, HarborFlow was trialed during an unusually harsh winter storm. Traditionally, the port would assign berths based on estimated arrival times, but during the storm, many ships were delayed unpredictably. HarborFlow integrated weather forecasts, vessel speed data, and crane availability to continually optimize the schedule. The result? A 15% increase in dock utilization and a 30% reduction in average wait time, even under severe conditions.

Jessamy Dunkham: That’s impressive. It sounds like it also reduces human error?

Xanthe Peltham: Yes, that’s a big plus. One of the anecdotes I like is from the Port of Linos, where a dockmaster told me that before HarborFlow, they’d spend hours each morning juggling spreadsheets and radios to update schedules. Now, the system flags potential conflicts and suggests adjustments instantly, freeing staff to focus on exceptions and on-the-ground issues.

Jessamy Dunkham: Are there any downsides or challenges with deploying these systems?

Xanthe Peltham: Integrating legacy systems is always tricky. Many ports still rely on outdated telemetry or siloed customs databases, so data quality and interoperability can be hurdles. Also, there’s a cultural shift—dock workers and schedulers need training and trust in AI recommendations. But we’re seeing growing acceptance as benefits become clear.

Jessamy Dunkham: Before we wrap up, any predictions on where dockside scheduling will be in five years?

Xanthe Peltham: I expect tighter integration across the entire maritime supply chain—from vessel tracking to inland logistics. Scheduling won’t just optimize berths but entire cargo flows, enabled by blockchain-verified data sharing and even more advanced machine learning. The goal? Near-zero idle time and seamless port operations.

Jessamy Dunkham: Fantastic insights, Xanthe. Thanks so much for sharing your expertise on The Embix Review.

Xanthe Peltham: My pleasure, Jessamy. Thanks for having me.
